the aortic valve in AS patients has a higher FDG uptake compared to healthy volunteers.
aortic valve fluorodeoxygluce (FDG) uptake is increased in aortic stensin, and that FDG uptake is associated with aortic valve calcification, but not aortic valve area.
aortic stenoses are associated with increased fluorodeoxygluce (FDG) uptake in the aortic valve, and that the severity of stenosis is associated with the degree of FDG uptake.

the study of the effects of the use of fluorodeoxyglu- cose (FDG) on the aortic valve.
the study of the effects of the presence of aortic regurgitation on the aortic valve.
the development and application of a new imaging method for the detection of coronary artery disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of F18-FDG PET/CT in aortic valve disease is still experimental and not yet established as a routine diagnostic tool.

the use of F-18-FDG-PET/CT is not recommended in patients with AS, but that it may be considered as a diagnostic tool to exclude aortic valve infection in the presence of aortic valve vegetation in patients with aortic valve endocarditis.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the imaging of the aortic valves using fluorodeoxy-glucose positron emission computed tomography (FDG-PET) increased the valvular FDG uptake in aortic valve stenosis (AS) in comparison to normal aortic valves.
we have demonstrated that FDG PET/CT imaging is a promising technique to assess aortic valve inflammation in patients with aortic stenoses.

The main takeaway from our work is that
FDG PET/CT imaging is a useful tool for the detection of valvular inflammation and can potentially be used as a non-invasive marker for valvular degeneration.

FDG PET imaging of the aortic valves in AS patients can be used to assess valvular metabolism and may help identify those patients with aortic valve disease who will benefit from transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI).
